questions.question: How do generators differ from regular functions?
questions.answer: generators uses function names as parameter while normal function use values as parameters
questions.feedback: This answer needs work. You covered 1/10 key concepts. Focus on: yield, lazy, iterator, next, suspend.
questions.model_answer: Generators use `yield` to produce values lazily, suspending between yields and keeping their state. `next()` resumes until the next yield. This makes them memory-efficient for large or infinite sequences. Generator expressions `(x for x in ...)` are a concise form.

questions.question: Explain list comprehensions with an example.
questions.answer: list comprehension is the short form of creating a function
questions.feedback: This answer needs work. You covered 1/10 key concepts. Focus on: expression, iterable, condition, syntax, concise.
questions.model_answer: A list comprehension builds a list in one expression: `[expression for item in iterable if condition]`. Example: `[x**2 for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0]` gives `[0,4,16,36,64]`. They're faster than loops and also work for sets, dicts, and generators.

questions.question: Explain Python's GIL (Global Interpreter Lock).
questions.feedback: This answer needs work. You covered 0/10 key concepts. Focus on: gil, thread, mutex, cpython, bytecode.
questions.model_answer: The GIL is a mutex in CPython letting only one thread run bytecode at a time, because reference counting isn't thread-safe. It's released during I/O, so threads help I/O-bound code, but CPU-bound work needs multiprocessing or C extensions to bypass it.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a list and a tuple in Python.
questions.answer: list is mutable data type i python while tuple is unmutable and we decalre ist with []  and tuple with ()
questions.feedback: This answer needs work. You covered 3/10 key concepts. Focus on: immutable, hashable, dictionary key, sequence, memory.
questions.model_answer: Lists (`[]`) are mutable; tuples (`()`) are immutable and hashable, so they can be dict keys/set elements. Tuples are slightly faster and smaller. Use lists for dynamic collections and tuples for fixed records; a one-element tuple needs a trailing comma `(1,)`.
